The overwhelming consensus across retrieved sources is that raw or abstract ideas cannot be patented. [d1] states plainly that "the short answer is no" to whether ideas can be patented, explaining that "neither copyrights or patents protect ideas." [d2] similarly confirms that "the government won't patent an idea. It doesn't matter how revolutionary and creative that idea is." [d3] echoes this, stating "the simple answer is no—you cannot patent an idea for an invention," and that the invention itself must be produced or a patent application filed with the USPTO. [d5] lists "abstract ideas" among things that "can never be patented, regardless of how well they meet" other criteria, and [d6] (from the USPTO itself) cites Supreme Court authority that "a new abstract idea is still an abstract idea" and remains unpatentable. [d7] (New York Times, citing Supreme Court rulings) further confirms that "abstract ideas and fundamental economic practices cannot be patented, because they are basic tools of scientific and technological activity." However, [d4] and [d10] add an important nuance: when an idea is sufficiently concrete, specific, and developed into a tangible invention with a described embodiment — a "reduction to practice" — it may qualify for patent protection, consistent with the other sources' distinction between a raw idea and a developed invention.
